safety.title: Safety
safety.description: How Oomba Academy keeps kids safe: games in a locked box, every game checked, chat only with real-life friends.
safety.heading: How we keep Oomba Academy safe

box.h: Games are kept in a box
box.p1: Every game runs in a locked box (a sandbox). Games cannot reach the internet, cannot see your account, and cannot open other pages.

checked.p1: A robot checker reads every version of every game. Games for everyone also get a careful review before anyone else can play them.
checked.p2: If something slips through, tap 🚩 Report on the game page. When three people report a game, it is hidden until our team looks.

chat.p1: You can only chat with people you added using their secret friend code. Chat blocks bad words, phone numbers, emails, addresses and links.
chat.p2: You can block or report anyone, any time. Grown-ups can turn chat off on the Me page.

personal.p1: We never ask you for your email, age or address, or for your real name (your school may add it to its class list). Pick a fun made-up name.

ads.p1: There are no ads on Oomba Academy. Nothing is for sale, and nothing pops up over a game.
ads.paid1: There are no ads on Oomba Academy. Playing is always free. You never have to pay for anything here, and nothing pops up over a game.

parents.title: For grown-ups
parents.description: What Oomba Academy is, what data it keeps, how friends and chat work, and how the AI Builder stays kid-safe.
parents.heading: For grown-ups

what.p1: A free website where kids play web games and build their own by describing them to an AI Builder. No downloads, no purchases, no loot boxes, no in-game money that costs money.
what.paid1: A website where kids play web games and build their own by describing them to an AI Builder. Playing is free, and so is a daily allowance of Builder messages. Families and schools can buy extra Builder messages. There are no in-game purchases, no loot boxes and no in-game money that costs money.

plans.p1: Free to build, with extra Builder messages for families and schools.
plans.p2: Plans and payments are covered by our Terms of Service, our Refund and Cancellation Policy and our Privacy Policy.

stored.p1: Own accounts keep a made-up name, a password (stored scrambled) and what your child does here: the games they make, their chats with the Builder and any pictures or files they add, saves, scores, ratings, favorites, friends, chat messages, a profile photo if they upload one, and settings such as language and theme. Guest play keeps a made-up name, saves, scores, ratings and favorites.
stored.p2: A school account is one your child signs in to with a login card from school. It is made and owned by the school, and keeps the same things plus the student's real name as the school typed it for the class list (only the school's staff and our team see it), their classes, lesson progress, written answers and their teacher's feedback. If your child joins a class with their own account and a class code, the school keeps the same things for that class, including their real name if the teacher types one.
stored.paid3: Family plans never see class activity: a grown-up linked to a student sees only that student's family extra messages.

never.p1: We never ask for an email address, age, home address, location or payment details, and there is nothing to buy. Hidden location data is removed from photos and pictures before they are kept. There are no ads, and no advertising or tracking cookies.
never.paid1: We never ask children for an email address, age, home address, location or payment details, and children are never asked to pay. A grown-up can choose a plan, and payment goes through Stripe; we never see card numbers. Hidden location data is removed from photos and pictures before they are kept. There are no ads, and no advertising or tracking cookies.

ai.p1: To make a game, the messages, pictures and files your child gives the Builder are sent to Claude, an AI made by the company Anthropic, which writes the game. Your child's name and username are not sent with them. Profile photos are also sent to Claude to be checked before anyone sees them. Claude reviews games before they can be shared with everyone, and our team checks any it is unsure about. Chats between friends and lesson answers are not sent to the AI.
ai.p2: Speaking instead of typing: when your child taps the microphone in the Builder chat, the recording is sent to {provider}, a speech-to-text service, which turns it into words. Your child sees the words and can change them before sending. The recording is used only for this and deleted straight away: we never store it, and {provider} is not allowed to keep it or use it to train its systems. The words go through the same safety checks as a typed message.
ai.p3: Looking up facts: to get a game right, the Builder can look up a fact on the web (for example how fast a cheetah runs). Your child never sees the web pages or links. The Builder is told never to search for anything personal; if a search still looks personal, its results are not used and its words are not kept. Adult, gambling, social media and video sites are blocked. We keep a list of the searches, without your child's name or username, together with the game they were for, for 90 days so our team can check them.

keep.p1: We keep an account's data for as long as the account exists. None of it is deleted on a timer yet. A game your child deletes is taken off the site for everyone, but a copy stays on our server.
keep.p2: There is no button yet to delete an account or download its data. To ask for either, a grown-up can contact us. For a school account, ask the school; it can ask us.
keep.madeP2: There is no button yet to delete an account or download its data, except that a grown-up who made their child's account can delete it from their family page. To ask for a deletion or a copy of the data, a grown-up can contact us. For a school account, ask the school; it can ask us.
keep.paid1: We keep an account's own data for as long as the account exists, and none of it is deleted on a timer yet. A game your child deletes is taken off the site for everyone, but a copy stays on our server. Family links, link codes and billing records have their own timers: see how long we keep billing information.

friends.p1: Friends are added only by a 6-character friend code, never by searching names. Chat is text between accepted friends only, filtered for bad language and personal details, rate-limited, and reportable. You can switch chat off on the Me page.

builder.p1: The Builder follows fixed kid-safety rules: no gore, no horror jump-scares, no gambling, no real brands or real people, no chat or data collection inside games, no links out. Requests that break the rules are kindly refused.

languages.p1: Pick a language with the 🌐 button at the top of any page or on the Me page. The Builder answers in that language and writes the words inside new games in it too. The same safety filters check every message, in every language.

families.p1: A parent or guardian can make their own grown-up account and link it to their child's account. Your child has to say yes on their own page.

made.h: If you make your child's account
made.p1: On your family page you can make your child's own account instead of linking one they already have. Your child signs in with the made-up name and password you choose.
made.li1: It is your child's account. Please don't chat or play as them: friends think they are talking to your child.
made.li2: You see counts only (games, uploads, saves, scores, friends, chat messages sent, which browsers are signed in), up to yesterday. Never what your child made, wrote or said.
made.li3: Your child is told that a grown-up made the account and what you can see. They can unlink or report you on their Me page, and then pick a new password.
made.li4: Before you make it, you read what the account keeps and tick that you are the child's parent or legal guardian. That, and paying for a plan, is not a parental consent check under children's privacy laws.
made.li5: You can change the password, see what we keep and delete the account from your family page. We keep it until you delete it: there are no automatic deletion timers yet.

sdk.title: For builders
sdk.description: The small helper every Oomba Academy game gets: saving, scores, effects, sounds and the player's language.
sdk.heading: Game SDK

brb.p1: Every game gets a small helper called BRB. {get} and {set} save progress for each player. localStorage also works and is saved to the cloud.
brb.p2: {submit} adds to the leaderboard (best score only). {over} ends a round.
brb.p5: {lang} is the player's language (like "fr" or "ar") and {dir} is "rtl" for right-to-left languages, so a game can speak the player's language.

rules.p1: Games cannot use the internet, cookies, forms, pop-ups or links. Fonts from Google Fonts and libraries from cdnjs are allowed. Keep each game under 2 MB.

who.p1: Oomba Academy (oomba.ai) is an educational website where kids aged 8 to 14, their families and their teachers play web games and build their own games with an AI "Builder".
who.p2: The service is run by Oomba Academy ("Oomba Academy", "we", "us"). You can reach us at {email}.
who.p3: These terms are the rules for using the site. They apply to everyone who uses it. Our Privacy Policy and our Refund and Cancellation Policy are part of these terms.
who.p4: A note for kids: these terms are written for grown-ups. The short version for you is on the Safety page: be kind, keep personal details private, only build games that follow the Builder's rules, and tell a grown-up you trust if anything worries you.

rules.h: 4. Using Oomba Academy safely: the rules
rules.p1: These rules apply to everyone, including what you type into the Builder, the games you make, chat messages, pictures you upload and your profile.
rules.li1: share personal details (yours or anyone else's): real full names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, school names in public places, or social media handles;
rules.li2: bully, threaten, harass or be mean to anyone;
rules.li3: make or share anything with gore, horror jump-scares, adult content, hate, gambling, drugs, or real weapons used to hurt people;
rules.li4: use real brands, real people, or other people's characters, music or art you don't have the right to use;
rules.li5: try to get around the safety filters, the Builder's rules, the game sandbox, or the message limits (for example with many accounts);
rules.li6: make games that collect data, chat, or link out of the site;
rules.li7: try to break, overload, scrape or attack the site, or get into accounts that are not yours;
rules.li8: buy or try to buy a plan with a payment card you are not allowed to use.
rules.li9: Every Builder message is screened before the AI sees it. Messages that break the rules are kindly refused.
rules.li10: A robot checker reads every version of every game. Games shared with everyone also get a careful review by an AI model, and a person on our team checks any game it is unsure about. Games shared with a class or school are checked before they reach that audience.
rules.li11: Chat is text only, only between friends who added each other by friend code, and filtered for bad language and personal details.
rules.li12: Anyone signed in can report a game. When three people report a game, it is hidden until our team looks. Anyone can block or report a chat partner.
rules.li13: Our team can approve, reject, hide or take down games, and pause, suspend or ban accounts. We log every moderation action.
rules.p2: No checking is perfect. If you see something wrong, please report it or email {email}.

ai.li1: The Builder uses Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, to write games from what you describe. What the AI makes can be wrong, buggy, or unexpectedly similar to something that already exists.
ai.li2: We check games before they are shared widely (section 4), but we do not promise that every game is free of mistakes.
ai.li3: Do not rely on games or AI answers for anything important (health, safety, money, homework answers you have not checked).
ai.li4: What you send to the Builder (messages, pictures, files) is sent to Anthropic to make the game. See our Privacy Policy for details.

games.li2: parts written by the AI may not be protected by copyright at all.
games.p3: So we can run the site, you give Oomba Academy a worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free licence to store, copy, run, show, take screenshots of, check (with people and AI tools, including sending the game to Anthropic for review), and make small technical changes to (for example to fit a screen or fix a safety problem) the games, pictures and text you put on the site, only to run, protect and improve Oomba Academy and only to show them to the people you chose (only me, friends, your classes, your school, or everyone).

plans.s1: 7.1 What is free and what you pay for
plans.li1: Playing is free for everyone, and so is a free daily allowance of Builder messages.
plans.li2: Paid plans only add more Builder messages. Paying never unlocks a feature that free users don't have.
plans.li3: Children never see prices or plans, and are never asked to pay. Only grown-up accounts and school admins can buy a plan.
plans.li4: We can change the size of the free allowance at any time. We will announce a change on the For grown-ups page before it applies.
plans.li5: Bought by a grown-up account for up to 4 linked children (each child must have confirmed the link).
plans.li6: Monthly or yearly, at the price shown to the grown-up before they buy.
plans.li7: It gives the family a set number of extra Builder messages each month, shared by the linked children, on top of each child's free daily messages. The number is shown before you buy and on your family page afterwards.
plans.li8: Each child uses their free daily messages first; extras are used after that, or when the free Builder is resting.
plans.li9: Extras reset at the start of each calendar month (UTC) and do not roll over. A "Pro quality" message counts as 2. A message that fails to build is given back.
plans.li10: To stop one child using the whole month in a day, there is a limit on how many extra messages one child can use in a day, and a limit on unusually expensive use.
plans.li11: A child in a school with a paid School plan builds from the school's allowance in class, never from the family's extras.
plans.li12: Family plans are for US families for now. You need a US billing address and a US payment card (or Apple Pay or Google Pay).
plans.li13: Priced per student per year, with a minimum of 25 students. The price is shown to the school's admins on the school's Billing tab.
plans.li14: The school gets a shared pool of Builder messages for its students and teachers each year. The size is shown on the school's Billing tab. Students always get at least the free daily amount. When the pool runs out, students use the free allowance until the next year starts.
plans.li15: Paid seats count active students. If you add students during the year, you can add seats: you pay a prorated amount for the rest of the year right away. You can lower the number of seats for the next year; the change applies at renewal, never below 25.
plans.li16: Paying: by card online, or by invoice (a purchase order is fine). Invoices are due 30 days after they are sent (net 30) and can be paid by card, bank transfer or ACH, or by check (email us for the mailing address).
plans.li17: Tax-exempt schools can send us their exemption certificate.
plans.li18: Payments are processed by Stripe. You pay on Stripe's own page. We never see or store your card number.
plans.li19: Prices are in US dollars and don't include sales tax. Where the law requires it, tax is added at checkout or on the invoice.
plans.li20: Stripe sends your receipts. The charge shows on your statement as OOMBA ACADEMY.
plans.li21: A monthly Family plan renews every month, and a yearly plan every year, at the price then in effect (see 7.7), charged to the payment method on file.
plans.li22: Before you pay, the checkout page shows the price, how often you'll be charged, and that it renews until you cancel. By paying, you agree to the automatic renewal.
plans.li23: We send a reminder before a yearly plan renews.

refunds.heading: Refund and Cancellation Policy

intro.p1: This page explains how to cancel an Oomba Academy plan and when you can get your money back. It is part of our Terms of Service.
intro.p2: Playing and the free daily Builder messages are always free. This policy is only about the paid Family and School plans, which add more Builder messages.

cancel.li1: Cancel anytime. There is no cancellation fee.
cancel.li2: Families: sign in to your grown-up account, open your family page, choose Manage billing, then cancel on Stripe's page. We ask for your password first.
cancel.li3: Schools: a school admin opens the school's Billing tab and chooses Manage billing, or emails {email} (invoice schools).
cancel.li4: When it takes effect: at the end of the month or year you already paid for. Until then the plan keeps working. After that, your family or school goes back to the free allowance.
cancel.li5: Nothing is deleted. Games, saves and classes stay exactly as they are.

refunds.p1: Full refund within 14 days. If you ask within 14 days of the payment that starts a plan, or of a yearly renewal, we refund that payment in full, including any tax charged.
refunds.p2: Monthly renewals are not refunded. You can cancel a monthly plan at any time so the next renewal doesn't happen.
refunds.p3: Otherwise, no partial refunds. If you cancel later, the plan simply runs to the end of the period you paid for. We don't refund unused days or unused messages.
refunds.p4: What a refund does: a refund ends the plan straight away (we cancel it first, then refund), so the extra messages stop at once.
refunds.p5: How to ask: email {email} from any address. Tell us the name of your grown-up account (or school), and the date and amount from your Stripe receipt. We'll reply within 3 business days.
refunds.p6: When you get the money: the refund goes back to the card or account you paid with. Banks usually take 5 to 10 business days to show it.
refunds.p7: Schools paying by invoice: the 14 days start on the date the payment reaches us. Paid by check? We refund by check or bank transfer.

special.li1: Paid twice by mistake? If two plans start for the same family or school, we cancel the extra one and refund it automatically.
special.li2: Payment didn't go through? Cards: the plan keeps working for 7 days while the payment is retried. Invoices: until 30 days after the due date. After that the plan ends and you're back on the free allowance. Nothing is deleted.
special.li3: A child used your card without asking? Email us right away. We will cancel the plan and, if you ask within 14 days of the payment, refund it in full.
special.li4: Disputed the charge with your bank? We end the plan straight away so the card isn't charged again. Please email us first; we can usually fix it faster.
special.li5: If we end your plan for a reason that isn't your fault, or we close Oomba Academy, we refund the unused part of the period you paid for.
special.li6: We may give a refund in other cases if we choose. Doing so once doesn't mean we must do it again.

rights.p1: This policy doesn't take away any refund rights you have under the law where you live.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: What Oomba Academy keeps, what it never collects, what the AI sees, and how grown-up accounts, payments and school billing work.
privacy.heading: Privacy Policy

intro.p1: This policy explains what Oomba Academy (oomba.ai, "we", "us") keeps about the people who use it, what we never collect, and how grown-up accounts, family links, payments and school billing work. The same facts about children's accounts are on the For grown-ups page. Questions: {email}.

grownups.li1: the name you type when you sign up (it can be a first name or nickname; children never see it: they see only "your grown-up");
grownups.li2: your password, stored scrambled (we can't read it);
grownups.li3: that you ticked "I am a parent or guardian, 18 or older" (we don't check this);
grownups.li4: your sign-in sessions, including your browser's name (user agent), and when you last re-entered your password for a billing step;
grownups.li5: which children you linked, when, and whether a link is pending, linked or ended;
grownups.li6: your plan: Stripe's customer and subscription numbers, plan type, monthly or yearly, status, seats, dates and amounts;
grownups.li7: a record of important actions (for example "plan started", "child linked", "refund"). These records never contain card details or email addresses.
grownups.p1: What we don't ask for: your email, phone number, home address or age. (Stripe asks for some of these when you pay: see Payments below.)
grownups.p2: A grown-up account can't build, chat, add friends or have a public profile, and doesn't appear in search.

linking.li7: The code: your child gets a short code on their Me page. We store it scrambled. It works once, for 24 hours.
linking.li2: The child says yes: the link only starts when your child confirms it on their own page. They can say No, or Report it to our team. Reports are kept while open and deleted 1 year after we close them.
linking.li3: What you see about your child: their username and display name, how many of the family's extra Builder messages they used yesterday and so far this month, and whether they are building on the Family plan or the free allowance.
linking.li4: What you don't see: today's live activity (so you can't tell when they're online), their chats, friends or games, any messages charged to a school, or whether they are in a school at all.
linking.li5: What your child sees about you: only the words "your grown-up", never the name you typed.
linking.li6: Counting messages: to count the family's extras, we record for each Builder message which allowance paid for it (free, family or school), how many messages it counted as, and its AI cost.

payments.p1: Payments are handled by Stripe, Inc. You pay on Stripe's own page, not on ours. Stripe's privacy policy is at stripe.com/privacy.
payments.p2: What Stripe collects from you (on Stripe's pages):
payments.li1: your email address (Stripe sends receipts, failed-payment notices and renewal reminders to it);
payments.li2: your card details, or your Apple Pay or Google Pay wallet;
payments.li3: your billing address (needed for sales tax and to check that family plans are for US families);
payments.li4: information Stripe uses to prevent fraud, such as details about your device and connection.
payments.p3: What we send to Stripe for a family plan: a random family number so we can match the payment to your plan. We do not send Stripe your name, your child's name or username, or anything about how your child uses the site. For schools, see School billing below.
payments.p4: What we get back and keep: Stripe's customer and subscription numbers, the plan, status (active, past due, cancelled), dates, amounts, seat count, and whether a payment was paid, failed, refunded or disputed.
payments.p5: What we never see or keep: your full card number or security code. For a family plan, our own database does not store your email or billing address. Stripe's messages to our server can include them, but we don't save them. A school's invoice request is different: see School billing below.
payments.p6: Who on our side can see more: the owner can see your email, billing address, receipts and the last 4 digits of your card in Stripe's dashboard. We use them only to run your plan: to answer your questions, give refunds, and tell you about important changes to your plan, price or our terms. The site has no email system of its own, so these notices are sent from {email} to the email Stripe holds. We never use it for marketing.
payments.p7: Fraud and disputes: if your bank reports a payment as disputed or likely fraud, Stripe tells us. We end the plan and keep a record of what happened.
payments.p8: Sales tax: Stripe calculates sales tax from your billing address where we are required to collect it.
payments.p9: Cookies: our site adds no new cookies for payments. Stripe's pages are run by Stripe and follow Stripe's policy.

schoolBilling.li1: Who sees it: only the school's admins and our team. Teachers and students never see billing.
schoolBilling.li2: What we keep when a school asks for an invoice: the number of seats, purchase order number, the billing contact's name and email, the school's billing address, whether the school says it is tax-exempt, and any note.
schoolBilling.li3: What goes to Stripe: when we create the school's invoices, the school's name, the billing contact's email, the billing address and the purchase order number are saved with Stripe, which sends the invoices. The contact's name, the note and the tax-exempt answer stay only with us. Nothing is sent until we create the invoices. A school that pays by card types its name and billing address on Stripe's page instead.
schoolBilling.li4: How long: the contact's name and email, the address, the note and the purchase order number in our database are deleted 2 years after the request is closed. Stripe keeps the school's address and purchase order number with its invoices (see below).
schoolBilling.li5: Seats are counted from the number of active students. Billing does not use students' names or work.
schoolBilling.li6: Families never see class activity: a grown-up linked to a student sees only that student's family extra messages.
schoolBilling.li7: Asking for a School plan: a teacher can ask their school's admins for a School plan. We keep which teacher asked, for which school and when, never a message. The school's admins see who asked until they dismiss it or the school gets a plan, and we delete it 90 days after that. Teachers only see whether their school has a plan.

schoolSetup.li1: What we keep when a teacher or school leader asks us to set up a school (the form on our teachers page): the school's name, their role, their work email, about how many students, the country, the language of the page and when it was sent. If they were signed in to a grown-up or school staff account, we also keep which account sent it. A guest's account is never kept with a request.
schoolSetup.li2: What we use it for: only to set up the school and reply to the request. We don't send newsletters, and we don't share it with Stripe or anyone else.
schoolSetup.li4: How long: deleted 1 year after we close the request (or 1 year after it was sent, if it is never closed).

children.p1: Children never see prices, plans or a "buy" button, and are never asked to pay or to ask a grown-up to pay.
children.p2: Paying is not how we ask a parent for permission. Buying a plan doesn't change what we collect about a child, what we use it for, or what a parent has agreed to.
children.p3: Your rights as a parent (own accounts): you can ask us to show you what we keep about your child, to delete it, or to stop collecting more. Email {email}. There is no delete or download button yet, so we handle these requests by hand, and we will need to check that you are the parent before we act. Unlinking or cancelling a plan does not delete your child's account.
children.p4: School accounts: a school account is made and owned by the school. For those accounts we act on the school's behalf and under its direction: we use student information only to provide Oomba Academy to the school, never for advertising, and we don't sell it. Parents of school accounts should ask the school to see or delete records; the school can ask us. A data agreement the school has signed with us comes first.
children.p5: No selling, no ads: we don't sell anyone's personal information, show ads, or use advertising or tracking cookies.

billingKeep.h: How long we keep billing information
billingKeep.li1: Link codes: deleted 30 days after they are used or expire.
billingKeep.li2: Pending links: deleted when they expire (24 hours) or the child says No.
billingKeep.li3: Ended links: deleted 90 days after they end (a record with account numbers only stays in our action log).
billingKeep.li4: Link reports: kept while open, then 1 year after they are closed.
billingKeep.li5: Plan and payment records (Stripe numbers, amounts, dates) and Stripe's invoices: 7 years, for tax law, even after an account is deleted.
billingKeep.li6: School invoice requests' contact details, address, note and purchase order number: 2 years after the request is closed.
billingKeep.li7: Grown-up account, family and links: until you ask us to delete the account. We cancel any plan first.

where.p1: Family plans are for US families for now.

more.p1: Grown-up accounts, family links, payments, school billing and how long we keep billing records are explained in the full privacy policy for grown-ups and schools.

made.h: Accounts a grown-up makes for a child
made.p1: A parent or legal guardian with a grown-up account can make their child's own account on their family page. It is an ordinary child's account, with the same rules, limits and safety checks as any other.
made.li1: What it keeps: the same as any child's account: games, Builder chats, pictures and files uploaded, game saves, scores, ratings and likes, friends and friend chat, a profile photo if one is added, settings, and sign-in cookies with the browser's name.
made.li8: What the grown-up sees: how many extra Builder messages the child used (up to yesterday), and counts of games, Builder chats, uploads, saves, scores, friends and chat messages sent, whether there is a profile photo, and which browsers are signed in. Never the content. The counts stop at the end of yesterday, so nothing the child adds today shows before tomorrow, but something the child deletes or ends today (a game, a friend, a sign-in) can already be missing from them.
made.li3: The grown-up chose the username and password. We ask them not to use the child's real name, and we refuse names that look like a real name, a birth year or the grown-up's own name.
made.li4: The child is told that a grown-up made the account and what that grown-up can see. They can unlink or report the grown-up on their Me page; that asks them for a new password, so the grown-up can't sign in as them any more.
made.li5: Before making the account, the grown-up reads a notice about what we keep and ticks that they have read it and that they are the child's parent or legal guardian. We keep a record of that: when, and which version of the notice. This is not a parental consent check under children's privacy laws, and we don't treat it as one. Paying for a plan isn't one either.
made.li9: The grown-up can see these counts and delete the account from their family page: everything the child made, wrote and uploaded goes straight away. We keep a short record that the account existed and who made it, the old username is held back for 90 days so nobody else can take it, and a class the child used to be in keeps its own records. If the child is in a school class now, the teacher removes them from the class first.
made.li7: How long: as long as the account exists. We have no automatic deletion timers yet.

learn.start: A round is each time the app asks the AI. It doesn’t remember, so the app sends it the chat again.
learn.look: This AI can read pictures, so it checks the screenshots for anything broken, blank or messy.
learn.scan: The safety program says exactly what was wrong, so the AI can fix just that part.
learn.retry: When a tool says something didn’t work, the AI reads why and tries another way.
learn.next: After each tool, the AI reads the result and picks the next step. That loop makes it an agent.
learn.thinking: Before it answers, this AI thinks quietly first, a bit like working something out in your head.
learn.long: Big ideas can take the AI a minute or two to plan before it writes any code. It keeps going even if you leave this page.
learn.msg: This AI reads new messages between steps, not in the middle of one. Then it can change its plan.

write.learn: The AI writes code one small piece at a time, each time predicting what should come next.

facts.a: AI reads and writes in tokens, which are small pieces of words. A long word can be several tokens.
facts.b: An AI writes by predicting the next token, again and again, very fast.
facts.c: Ask the same thing twice and you may get a different answer, because the AI picks from likely next words.
facts.d: Every round, the AI reads the recent chat again. That’s why long chats use more tokens.
facts.e: An agent is an AI that uses tools in a loop. This Builder can take up to 14 rounds for each build.
facts.f: The Builder AI can’t use the internet. It builds from what it learned and what you tell it.
facts.g: AI models learn patterns from huge amounts of writing and code made by people.
facts.h: AI can sound sure and still be wrong. That’s why a safety program checks the code too.
facts.i: ✨ Pro quality uses a bigger AI that thinks for longer: slower, but often better at tricky games.
facts.j: Always play your game yourself. Even clever AI misses things a real player would notice.
facts.k: You can send new ideas while the AI works. It reads them between its steps.

setup.heading: Sign in with Google for schools

what.p1: Students and staff can sign in to Oomba Academy with their school Google account, for example on a Chromebook. Oomba Academy only asks Google for basic sign-in information: the account's name and email address.

turnOn.h: Turn it on for your school
turnOn.p1: A school admin adds the school's Google Workspace domain on the school's Settings tab. Until then, nobody at the school can use Google sign-in.

trust.p1: Google lets students who are under 18 use an app only after the school's Google admin allows it. Otherwise they see “Access blocked”. Your Google admin can allow Oomba Academy like this (menu names may differ slightly):

setup.step1: Sign in to the Google Admin console (admin.google.com) as an admin.
setup.step2: Go to Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage third-party app access.
setup.step3: Add an app, and search for this client ID: {id}
setup.step4: Pick the organisational units with students (and staff), choose Trusted or Limited, and save.
setup.step5: Or: for users under 18, allow apps that only ask for the basic information needed for Sign in with Google.
setup.step6: It can take a little while to apply. Then ask a student to try “Sign in with Google” again.

invite.p1: On a class's Students tab, paste the students' school email addresses. When a student signs in with that Google account, they join the class. Nothing is emailed.
invite.p2: Or turn on “join with Google” next to the class code: students with a school Google account type the code and join at once.

privacy.p1: We keep the Google account's id, email address and school domain while it is connected, to recognise it at sign-in. We never store the Google photo, never show a student's Google name on the game site, and never use the account to read anything else from Google.

teachers.lead: Oomba Academy is a free website of learning games for ages 8 to 14. Students play right in the browser, and your class can make its own games by describing them to our AI Builder.

how.h: How it works in your classroom
how.lead: Real screens from a demo school with made-up names, from your class list to the gradebook.

s1.p: Once your school is set up, your school admin adds teachers, and each teacher makes their classes on My classes.
s1.alt: My classes for a teacher at Sunny Hill Demo School: three class cards, Coding Club, Ms. Rivera’s Class (5 students, 1 join request, 2 answers to review) and Reading Rockets, and a Lesson library button.

s2.h: Students join with a code or login cards
s2.p: Students with their own account join with the class code, and you approve them. No email needed: you can make school accounts and print login cards.
s2.pgoogle: Students with their own account join with the class code, and you approve them. No email needed: you can make school accounts and print login cards. Or they sign in with their school Google account.
s2.alt: A class’s Students tab: one student, @StarGecko, asks to join with the class code, with a box for their real name and Approve and Decline buttons. Below it, the class list of 5 students and a button for new login cards.

s3.p: Lessons mix short reading, a learning game, a build-a-game task and written questions. Assign one to a class with a due date.
s3.alt: The Steps list in the lesson editor: step 1, “Warm-up: slices of pizza”, and step 2, “Keep the bottom, add the top”, each with its text, its minutes and an Edit step button.

s4.p: Each student works through the lesson at their own pace on any device.
s4.alt: A student’s view of a lesson: the game step, Quick-math warm-up, is marked Done with a best score of 47 and a Play Sum Racer button. Next come a build-a-game step with a Start building button, then a written question, the Exit ticket.

s5.p: The gradebook shows each student’s progress, game scores and written answers. Leave feedback, or download it as a CSV.
s5.alt: The class Progress tab: a gradebook table with how many steps each student has done in each lesson, a Download (CSV) button and a link to the written answers waiting for review.

build.p1: Students describe a game in their own words, and the Builder makes it. While it works, it shows its steps behind the scenes, with short learning tips.
build.p2: Writing a clear idea, testing the game and asking for changes is planning, writing and debugging, without having to know code first.

safe.li1: No ads, and no advertising or tracking cookies.

faq.q1: Is Oomba Academy free for teachers?
faq.a1: Yes. Playing, classes, lessons and progress are free, and every student account gets free Builder messages each day.
faq.q2: Do students need an account or an email address to play?
faq.a2: No. Anyone can play straight away. For your classes you can make school accounts without any email address and print login cards for them.
faq.q3: Does it work on Chromebooks and school networks?
faq.a3: It runs in any up-to-date web browser, on Chromebooks, laptops, tablets and on the classroom board, with nothing to install. If your school filters websites, ask your IT team to allow {host}.
faq.q4: How do you protect student privacy?
faq.a4: We never ask students for an email address, age or home address. There are no ads and no tracking cookies, and a student's real name is seen only by their school's staff. Our privacy notice lists exactly what we keep.
faq.q5: What ages and grades is it for?
faq.a5: Oomba Academy is made for ages 8 to 14, roughly grades 3 to 8. Some games, such as Shark Plank and the first Sum Racer tracks, also suit younger readers.
faq.q6: How do I add my class?
faq.a6: First, email us to set up your school (it’s free). Then create a class and share its class code with students who have their own account, or make school accounts for the whole class and print login cards.
faq.a6google: First, email us to set up your school (it’s free). Then create a class and share its class code with students who have their own account, or make school accounts for the whole class and print login cards. Schools that use Google can let students sign in with Google.
faq.q7: Can students make their own games? Who sees them?
faq.a7: Yes. A new game is private to the student who made it. They can share it with their class, and a game for everyone is reviewed before anyone else can play it.
faq.q8: Can I track progress and scores?
faq.a8: Yes. Lessons record each student’s progress, game scores and written answers. You see them on the class’s Progress tab, and can download each student’s lesson progress as a spreadsheet (CSV).
faq.a9: {count} languages, including Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Arabic, Hebrew and Japanese. Each student picks their own.
faq.a4google: Students never type an email address, and we never ask for their age or home address. If your school uses Sign in with Google, we keep each student’s school Google email only to recognize their account. There are no ads and no tracking cookies. Our privacy notice lists exactly what we keep.

math.name: Math games
math.short: Addition, subtraction, multiplication (times tables) and division
math.title: Free math games: addition, subtraction, multiplication
math.description: Practice addition, subtraction, multiplication and division facts in Sum Racer, a free math racing game for grades 1 to 5, with two-player races.
math.lead: Sum Racer is a free math facts game: every right answer speeds a kart past the other racers. Pick the track that matches what your class is learning, from addition to 10 up to the times tables and division, and run a quick race at the start of a lesson. It works in the browser, on Chromebooks, tablets and the classroom board.

tracks.h: Seven tracks: addition and subtraction to 100, multiplication (times tables) to 12, division
tracks.li5: Multiplication: all the times tables up to 12
tracks.p: Students can also pick exactly which times tables to practice.

math.tips: Start a lesson with a five-minute race on the track you are working on, or put two students on one device for a head-to-head race.

faq.q1: What math does Sum Racer cover?
faq.a1: Addition to 10, addition and subtraction to 20 and 100, the times tables up to 12, division facts, and a mixed track with all four operations.
faq.q2: Can two students race each other?
faq.a2: Yes. Two players can race on one screen.
faq.a3: Yes. It is free to play, with no ads, and students can start without signing up.
faq.q4: Can my child practice just one times table at home?
faq.a4: Yes. In Sum Racer they can pick exactly which times tables to practice.

math.home: A five-minute race after school keeps math facts fresh. Pick the track your child is working on at school, or choose exactly which times tables to practice, and race each other on the same screen.

words.name: Reading and spelling games
words.short: Word searches, hangman and a daily word puzzle
words.title: Free reading and spelling games for kids
words.description: Word searches, hangman and a daily word puzzle for ages 8 to 14, with words read aloud for early readers. Free, no ads, in any browser.
words.h1: Reading and spelling games for early and growing readers
words.lead: Three word games that build spelling and vocabulary. Shark Plank and Word Hunt read words aloud, so they suit early readers. Word Peek is a daily word puzzle for confident spellers.
words.tips: Use a Word Hunt theme as a warm-up for a topic, solve the Daily Peek together on the board and talk about each guess, or set Shark Plank for early finishers.

faq.q1: Do the games read words aloud?
faq.a1: Shark Plank reads each word aloud, and in Word Hunt students can tap any word to hear it.
faq.a2: Yes. Word Hunt and Word Peek each have a new daily puzzle, and in Word Peek a student can set a secret word for a friend.
faq.q3: Can I use my own spelling list?
faq.a3: Not in these games yet. You can describe a spelling game with your words to the Builder, and it will make one for your class.
faq.q4: Which word game suits my child’s reading level?
faq.a4: Shark Plank and Word Hunt read words aloud, so they suit kids who are still building their reading. Word Peek is for confident spellers.

words.home: Make the Daily Peek a family habit at breakfast and talk about each guess, or let a younger reader play Shark Plank with the sound on, so every word is read aloud.

strategy.name: Chess and strategy games
strategy.short: Chess lessons and puzzles, four in a row, block puzzles
strategy.title: Free chess and strategy games for kids
strategy.description: Learn chess with short lessons and puzzles, then play a friend or a robot. Plus four in a row and falling-block puzzles, free for ages 8 to 14.
strategy.h1: Chess and strategy games that build thinking skills
strategy.lead: Strategy games ask students to plan ahead, spot patterns and think about what the other player will do. Castle Clash teaches chess from the first move. Drop Four and Brick Drop are quick games of planning and patterns.
strategy.tips: Run a class chess club with Castle Clash's lessons and puzzles, or pair students on one device for a game of Drop Four.

faq.q1: Can kids learn chess from scratch?
faq.a1: Yes. Castle Clash has a short lesson for every piece and 24 checkmate puzzles, then a robot to play at four levels.
faq.q2: Can two students play on one device?
faq.a2: Yes. Castle Clash and Drop Four both have a two-player mode on one screen.
faq.a3: Castle Clash's robot has four levels, and Drop Four's robot has Easy, Normal and Hard.
faq.q4: Can I learn chess alongside my child?
faq.a4: Yes. Castle Clash’s lessons start with how each piece moves, so a grown-up who has never played can learn too, then play their child on the same screen.

strategy.home: Learn chess together: do one Castle Clash lesson a day, then play each other on one screen. Drop Four fits into any spare five minutes.

music.h1: Music games: make beats and play along
music.lead: Loop Lab is a beat maker: students tap squares to build a loop of drums, bass and melody and hear it straight away. Beat Lanes is a rhythm game with nine songs, from Twinkle Twinkle to the Can-Can.
music.tips: Use Loop Lab's music challenges to explore patterns and repetition, or play a Beat Lanes song as a quick brain break. Headphones help in a busy room.

faq.q1: Do students need to read music?
faq.a1: No. Both games use colors and timing, not written notes.
faq.a2: Yes. In Loop Lab they can chain patterns into a song and play it back like a little concert.
faq.q3: Does my child need an instrument or music lessons?
faq.a3: No. Everything happens in the browser, with colors and timing instead of written notes.

music.home: Loop Lab needs no lessons and no instrument: kids make a beat, chain it into a song and play it back to the family. Headphones help in a busy house.

brainBreaks.description: Short, fun games for a 3 to 5 minute classroom brain break: rhythm, hoops, mazes, falling blocks and a daily word puzzle. Free, no ads, no sign-up.
brainBreaks.h1: Quick brain break games for the classroom
brainBreaks.lead: A few minutes of play between lessons helps students reset. These games start in seconds, need no sign-up, and are easy to stop when the timer ends.
brainBreaks.tips: Set a timer for 3 to 5 minutes, put a game on the board and let the class take turns, or let students play on their own devices.

faq.q1: How long should a brain break be?
faq.a1: Many teachers use 3 to 5 minutes. These games have short rounds, so it is easy to stop on time.
faq.q2: Can the whole class play on one screen?
faq.a2: Yes. Put a game on the board and take turns. Beat Lanes and Swish Flick work well with the class cheering along.

makeAGame.name: Make your own game
makeAGame.short: Kids design games with the AI Builder
makeAGame.title: Make your own video game: AI game maker for kids
makeAGame.description: Kids describe a game in plain words and the Builder makes it, showing its steps. No coding needed, ad-free, for ages 8 to 14, and private until shared.
makeAGame.h1: Make your own game, no coding needed
makeAGame.lead: On Oomba Academy, students describe the game they want and the AI Builder makes it. Then they play it, test it and ask for changes, one idea at a time.

how.li1: Describe: type an idea, like “a maze where a cat collects fish”, and add a drawing or photo if you like.
how.li2: Build: the Builder makes the game and shows its steps behind the scenes while it works.
how.li3: Play and test: try it out and notice what to change.
how.li4: Improve: ask for changes in plain words, one at a time.

skills.p: Planning an idea, writing clear instructions, testing, finding and fixing problems, and improving a design step by step: the habits of programmers and game designers.

safe.p: The Builder follows fixed kid-safety rules: no gore, no gambling, no real brands or real people, no chat or data collection inside games, and no links out. Every game runs in a locked sandbox.

makeAGame.tips: Add a “build a game” step to a lesson with the idea students start from. A project that works well: each student designs a review game for the topic you are teaching, then classmates play it and give feedback.

faq.q1: Do students need to know how to code?
faq.a1: No. They describe the game in their own words. The Builder shows its steps as it works, so curious students can see how a game is put together.
faq.q2: Who can see the games students make?
faq.a2: Only the student, until they share it. They can share it with friends or their class, and a game for everyone is reviewed before anyone else can play it.
faq.q4: My child wants to make video games. Where do they start?
faq.a4: With a small idea, like a maze or a catching game. They describe it, play it, then ask for one change at a time. Later, many kids also try coding tools like Scratch.
faq.a5: Not exactly. The Builder writes the code. Your child does the design, the testing and the explaining, which are big parts of making games, and the steps it shows let curious kids see how a game is put together.
faq.a6: Nothing. Every player with an account (just a made-up name and a password) gets free Builder messages each day.
faq.a6paid: Building is free: every player with an account (just a made-up name and a password) gets free Builder messages each day. Families and schools can choose an optional plan for extra messages. See the plans.
faq.q7: Is the AI Builder safe for my child?
faq.a7: It only makes games, and it follows fixed kid-safety rules in every language. Read what it sees and the rules it follows.

parents.h: For parents: why making beats only playing
parents.p1: Making a game is active screen time. Your child plans an idea, explains it clearly, tests what the Builder made and decides what to fix next: the same steps game designers use.
parents.p2: It makes a good weekend project to do together, and building is free every day.

ai.title: Is AI safe for kids? Our Builder, explained
ai.description: What the AI sees, what it never gets, and the rules it follows: a plain-words guide for parents of kids 8–14 using Oomba Academy’s AI game Builder.
ai.h1: Is the AI Builder safe for my child?
ai.lead: Oomba Academy’s Builder uses AI to turn your child’s idea into a game. Here is what it sees, what it never gets, the rules it follows and what we can’t promise, in plain words.

what.p1: The Builder makes games. Your child describes an idea, and it writes the game, shows its steps while it works and asks a question when it needs to know more.
what.p2: It is made for building games, not as a friend or companion to chat with about anything else.

sees.h: What the AI sees, and what it never gets
sees.li1: The messages, pictures and files your child gives the Builder go to Claude, an AI made by the company Anthropic, which writes the game.
sees.li2: Your child’s name and username are not sent with them.
sees.li3: Chats between friends and lesson answers are never sent to the AI.
sees.li4: Hidden location data is removed from photos and pictures before they are kept.
sees.li5: If your child uploads a profile photo, it is sent to Claude to be checked before anyone sees it.
sees.li6: Games your child wants to share with everyone are reviewed by Claude first.

rules.p: The Builder follows fixed kid-safety rules in every language, and a message can’t change them:
rules.li1: No blood, gore or realistic violence, and no horror or jump-scares. Cartoon slapstick is fine.
rules.li3: No real brands, and no real people as characters.
rules.li4: No chat between players and no collecting personal details inside games.
rules.li5: No links to other websites and no ads inside games.
rules.li6: No romantic or adult content, no bullying or hate, and nothing about self-harm, drugs, alcohol or vaping.
rules.li7: No copyrighted characters like Mario or Pokémon, and no real classmates, teachers or family members in games.
rules.p2: A request that breaks the rules is kindly refused, with ideas for something it can make instead.

public.p: A new game is private to your child. They can share it with friends or their class. A game for everyone is reviewed by Claude before anyone else can play it, and our team checks any it is unsure about. Every game runs in a locked sandbox that can’t reach the internet or your child’s account.

limits.p1: No filter is perfect. An AI can misunderstand a request or make a mistake, and a game could still have something that isn’t right for your child.
limits.p2: If you see something wrong, tap 🚩 Report on the game page. Enough reports hide a game until our team looks, and grown-ups can also email us at {email}.

check.h: Five questions to ask about any AI tool for kids
check.li1: What does it do? A tool that makes something (a game, a picture, a story) is different from a chatbot that talks about anything.
check.li2: What does it send, and to whom? Look for a plain list of what goes to the AI company, and whether your child’s name goes with it.
check.li3: What rules does it follow? A good tool for kids says what it refuses to make.
check.li4: Who sees what your child makes? Private until shared is safest.
check.li5: Can you report a problem? There should be an easy way, and a person who looks.

faq.q1: Does my child chat with an AI?
faq.a1: Only about the game they’re making. They describe what they want, and the Builder asks questions and explains its steps.
faq.q2: Is my child’s name sent to the AI?
faq.a2: No. Their name and username are not sent with their messages.
faq.q3: Can the AI make scary or violent games?
faq.a3: Games can have cartoon action, like a hero’s friendly battles, but the Builder refuses gore, realistic violence, horror and jump-scares. See every rule it follows.
faq.q4: Are the games my child makes public?
faq.a4: Not unless they share them. A game for everyone is reviewed before anyone else can play it.
faq.q5: Is the Builder a companion or a friend bot?
faq.a5: No. It is a tool for making games.

screen.short: A checklist for choosing games and apps, and how to set limits
screen.title: Good screen time for kids: a parent’s guide
screen.description: How to tell good screen time from bad: ads, purchases, chat, data, and making vs scrolling. A checklist for parents, with what we do and don’t do.
screen.h1: Good screen time: how to choose games for kids 8–14
screen.lead: There’s no perfect number of minutes. What kids do on a screen, who they do it with and what it pushes them toward matter just as much. This checklist helps you judge any game or app, including ours.

experts.p1: The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests a family media plan instead of one number for every child: for school-age kids, consistent limits that protect sleep, schoolwork, physical activity and time together. Common Sense Media also looks at the quality of what kids watch and play, not only the minutes.
experts.p2: So we won’t give you a number of minutes here: you know your child. We can help you judge what those minutes are spent on.

check.h: A checklist for any game or app
check.li1: Ads: does it show ads, or videos that lead to more videos?
check.li2: Purchases: can your child spend money? Is there in-game money, loot boxes or “pay to win”?
check.li3: Strangers: can people your child doesn’t know send them messages?
check.li4: Data: does it ask your child for an email address, age, location or photos?
check.li5: Age fit: is it made for your child’s age, not just allowed for it?
check.li6: Making or scrolling: does your child solve, practice or make something, or mostly watch?
check.li7: Together: can you play it with them?

us.h: How Oomba Academy does on it, honestly
us.li2: Purchases: nothing for kids to buy, no loot boxes and no in-game money that costs money.
us.li3: Strangers: chat only with friends added by a code, filtered and reportable.
us.li4: Data: we never ask kids for an email address, age, address or location. Photos are optional: a profile photo or pictures for the Builder, with hidden location data removed and profile photos checked before anyone sees them.
us.li6: Making: kids can make their own games with the AI Builder.
us.li7: Together: several games have a two-player mode on one screen.
us.p: What we don’t have: time limits, activity reports or a parent dashboard. For limits, use your device’s own tools.

tools.h: Setting limits with your device’s tools
tools.p: These free tools from the device makers let you set daily limits, downtime and app rules:
tools.li1: Apple Screen Time on iPhone, iPad and Mac
tools.li2: Google Family Link on Android phones, tablets and Chromebooks
tools.li3: Microsoft Family Safety on Windows and Xbox

rules.li1: Play a new game together the first time.
rules.li2: Keep building and chatting in a shared room.
rules.li3: Agree on when, not only how long: after homework, not at bedtime.
rules.li4: Ask what they made or learned today.
rules.li5: Use the same rules for every screen in the house, grown-ups’ too.

faq.q1: How much screen time is OK for a 10 year old?
faq.a1: There is no single number. Pediatricians suggest consistent limits that leave room for sleep, school, being active and family time, and paying attention to what kids do on screens. A family media plan helps you decide.
faq.q2: Is educational screen time better than games?
faq.a2: Games can be educational. Look for ones where your child solves, practices or makes something, with no ads or purchases pulling them along.
faq.q3: Does Oomba Academy have time limits?
faq.a3: No. Use your device’s tools, like Apple Screen Time, Google Family Link or Microsoft Family Safety.
faq.q4: Is making games better than playing them?
faq.a4: Both have a place. Making a game asks kids to plan, explain clearly, test and fix, so it is an active kind of screen time.
